blocks.text: In Revelation 22:19, ancient textual traditions differ: some read “tree of life,” while others read “book of life.” The difference is worth noticing because the warning concerns losing one’s share in what the book describes; readers may therefore encounter either wording in translations or notes. The chapter’s tree imagery also includes leaves “for the healing of the nations,” and its closing combines revelatory vision, prophecy, and a message intended for circulation among churches.

sections.title: A Textual Variation at the Close

blocks.text: The river and tree in the chapter’s opening belong to a larger pattern in which Revelation recomposes Ezekielian imagery—including throne, scroll, measuring, plague, battle, city, river, and tree—within its own literary sequence. This places the final vision within a sustained network of reused images rather than presenting its details as isolated symbols.

The New Jerusalem vision brings together several images: city, bride, sanctuary, Eden, and renewed Zion. More broadly, Revelation repeatedly reworks Israel’s Scriptures, including Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. The river and tree at the beginning of chapter 22 are therefore part of this layered portrayal of the city.

sections.title: Images Carried into the Final Vision
